newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zairean peace initiative on track in Cape Town.
newsitem.headline: Zairean peace initiative on track in Cape Town.

text.p: Zaire's warring parties inched toward their first talks in Cape Town on Thursday, but South African and foreign officials put a lid on all news about a possible breakthrough in their search for peace.
A South African government official said bluntly there would be no early word on the progress of the initiative and added that it could be days before any conclusion is announced.
In Kinshasa, Zaire's government issued a warning to civilians in rebel-held areas to leave ahead of a renewed bombing campaign.
"The Zairean army is determined to carry on the war in order to retake all the territory occupied by the invaders.
"Air raids will be carried out on all fronts until the total destruction of the enemy's military targets," the government said in a statement.
Zaire accuses neighbouring Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of backing rebels who took up arms in October, charging that the government was trying to expel ethnic Tutsis from Zaire.
Parks Mankahlana, spokesman for President Nelson Mandela, confirmed to Reuters the breakthrough peace initiative was on track, but added: "We are not releasing any details."
A U.S. official said Assistant-Secretary of State for African Affairs George Moose was in Cape Town on Thursday and spent the afternoon in talks with "South African counterparts".
Moose left his waterfront hotel later for what an official said would be "talks at an undisclosed location probably going on until late tonight".
Mandela revealed plans on Wednesday for a first meeting between the government of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila's forces.
But diplomats said on Thursday Mandela had erred in going public and that the meeting, which was to have taken place in secrecy, was under threat.
After initially having expanded on Mandela's announcement, South African officials clamped down through the day until, by nightfall, none was willing to talk about the initiative.

It was not clear at day's end if the rebels were represented by Kabila or by a substitute. Mobutu's nephew and chief security adviser Ngbanda Nzambo Ko Ayumba was in Cape Town, but some sources said a second government repesentative may be with him.
Pretoria's director general of foreign affairs, Rusty Evans, told Reuters after Mandela's announcement: "There is a great reluctance on both sides to acknowledge that they are willing to negotiate."
Government sources said Deputy President Thabo Mbeki was managing the process of drawing the two sides closer together.
The Zairean government has refused to talk to the rebels since fighting erupted.
Evans said South Africa would try to facilitate a first meeting between the government and the rebels, adding:
"We're more than willing and very pleased to provide a venue for them to meet. How they meet, how they conduct their meeting and what they choose to say about it is for them to decide."

The Cape Town initiative was opened in parallel with a meeting of African foreign ministers in Kinshasa, where they sought to draw the warring sides into a third Nairobi summit on United Nations proposals for a ceasefire and elections.

"The ministers also emphasised the African leaders' commitment to preserving Zaire's territorial integrity and to finding a peaceful means to resolve the crisis," they said in a statement after two days in the region.
Regional leaders have met twice in Nairobi with Mandela, widely seen as Africa's leading statesman, present at the second meeting.
